input:
A blackened plate that is held at a temperature of 800 K faces surroundings that are at a temperature of 300 K, and the aim here is to estimate the net radiative heat flux exchanged between the plate and those surroundings. The emissivity of the plate, denoted by $\varepsilon$, is 0.9. The governing relation is the Stefan-Boltzmann relation, in which $\sigma$ is the Stefan-Boltzmann constant, 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4, and the relation is written as follows:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

In this relation, $T_1$ is the plate temperature (800 K) and $T_2$ is the surroundings temperature (300 K), and when these values are substituted the net radiative heat flux $q$ is obtained as 20.5 kW m-2. It should be noted, however, that the estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel, and that the view factors appropriate to the real geometry have not been included, so the flux that has been calculated is the flux for that idealised arrangement rather than a description of an arrangement in which the surfaces might only partially face one another. It may also be observed that radiation of this kind depends very strongly on temperature, considerably more strongly than the modes of transfer that depend on a simple difference of temperatures, and this is one of the reasons why the plate, which is much the hotter of the two bodies involved in the exchange, contributes so overwhelmingly to the outcome of the calculation. The surroundings, for their part, also radiate towards the plate, and the net character of the flux that has been reported reflects the fact that both directions of exchange have been taken into account, with the emission from the plate exceeding the emission from the surroundings by the margin that the temperatures and the emissivity together produce. The treatment of the plate surface through its emissivity is likewise a simplification, in that the emissivity of a real surface can depend on the condition of the surface and on the direction in which the radiation leaves it, none of which has been gone into in the present estimate.
target:
A blackened plate at 800 K faces surroundings at 300 K. The emissivity $\varepsilon$ of the plate is 0.9. The net radiative heat flux $q$ follows from the Stefan-Boltzmann constant $\sigma$ = 5.67 x 10-8 W m-2 K-4 through the Stefan-Boltzmann relation:

$$q = \varepsilon \sigma (T_1^4 - T_2^4)$$

In the relation, $T_1$ is the plate temperature (800 K) and $T_2$ is the surroundings temperature (300 K). Substitution gives $q$ = 20.5 kW m-2. The estimate treats both surfaces as large and parallel; view factors for the real geometry are not included. The stated flux is therefore the exchange under the large parallel-surface idealisation, and an arrangement whose surfaces see each other only in part exchanges less, by the view factor the estimate omits. Radiation differs from the other modes in the temperatures it depends on. The relation takes each temperature to the fourth power, so the hotter body dominates the exchange out of proportion to the difference in kelvin: the plate term exceeds the surroundings term by a wide factor even though both bodies radiate, and a small change in the plate temperature moves the flux far more than the same change in the surroundings temperature. The emissivity scales the whole exchange. A surface that radiates less effectively than the plate considered here, at the same temperatures, exchanges proportionally less, while the temperatures themselves fix the ceiling that the emissivity scales down from. The estimate also holds both temperatures fixed, as the relation requires: it is an instantaneous flux for the stated pair of temperatures, not an average over a period in which the plate cools. A plate losing heat by radiation alone moves towards the surroundings temperature as it cools, and its flux falls steeply along the way, so the stated value describes the start of such a process and not its course. The estimate is likewise a statement about the pair of surfaces as arranged. Move the same plate to surroundings it faces only obliquely, or screen part of its view, and the exchange falls even though every quantity named in the relation keeps its value.
